title: Event subscriptions and object lifetime
body: A publisher's event holds a delegate, and the delegate holds a strong reference to the subscriber object whose method it calls. If a long-lived publisher (a static event, an application-wide service, a timer) keeps that subscription, the subscriber can never be garbage collected, even after everything else has forgotten it. This is the most common managed-memory leak in C# programs.

The example shows it deterministically. A `Window` subscribes to a long-lived `Clock` and is then dropped. A `WeakReference` observes whether the window object is still alive after a full, blocking garbage collection. While subscribed, it survives; after unsubscribing, it is collected.

The window is created inside a separate non-inlined method so no local variable in the caller keeps it reachable; debug builds otherwise extend local lifetimes to the end of a method. `GC.Collect()` and `GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers()` are used only to make the demonstration observable; production code should not call them.

Fixes, in order of preference: unsubscribe when the subscriber's lifetime ends, usually in `Dispose` (stage 10) so a `using` guarantees it; return an `IDisposable` subscription token from the publisher so callers cannot forget the matching `-=`; or use a weak-event pattern for frameworks where explicit unsubscription is impractical. Unsubscribing requires the same delegate instance, so store a lambda in a field if you need to remove it later.
When a subscriber lives shorter than its publisher, check where its subscription ends. Static events deserve special suspicion because their publisher lives for the whole process.
expectedStdout:
subscribed window alive: True
unsubscribed window alive: False
clock subscribers: 1
challenge: Change the publisher so Subscribe(EventHandler handler) returns an IDisposable token whose Dispose removes the handler. Show subscriber counts before and after disposing the token with a using block.
question: Why can a subscriber stay in memory after the rest of the program drops it?
correct: The publisher's event delegate still references the subscriber
wrong: Events pin objects so the GC cannot move them
The finalizer queue keeps all subscribers
reasoning: Delegates hold their target strongly, so a longer-lived publisher keeps subscribers reachable until they unsubscribe.
